The Quantum Leap: Why We Care About Qubits

Alright, let’s get started! Today, we are going to dive into the weird, wild, and incredibly useful world of photon polarization and quantum states. Over the next couple of lectures, we are going to unpack the things that make qubits behave in ways that seem non-intuitive at first glance. My goal is to make this as intuitive as possible for you, because this is the foundation for some truly amazing technology.

Last time, we talked about why we even bother with this whole quantum mumbo jumbo. On one hand, we have our handy classical bits—the ones storing data in the cloud, on our phones, and in our laptops. At the end of the day, each classical bit stores exactly one value: a 0 or a 1.

But we saw that a quantum bit, or qubit, can store multiple values at the same time. If you put two qubits together, they can store four numbers simultaneously. Three qubits can store eight values, and so on. The scaling is exponential. We saw that with just about 50 qubits, you can store something like a quadrillion values—thousands or millions of times greater than the entire world population! In a nutshell, that exponential power is why the scientific community is going gaga over quantum computing.

The Anatomy of a Quantum State

Let’s do a quick review and formalize how we write these things down. A qubit, or a quantum state, is essentially a superposition (or linear combination) of two basic states.

To write this down, you will notice I always use this strange half-bracket notation with a vertical line and an angled bracket, like this: |\psi\rangle. This is called ket notation. It is standard speak in quantum mechanics and quantum chemistry. (If you take advanced physics, you might see its partner, the "bra" \langle \psi |, which together make a "bra-ket", but for our purposes, we are just going to hang out with the ket).

Let’s define our generic quantum state, |\psi\rangle, as a linear combination of two bits, |0\rangle and |1\rangle:

\begin{equation} |\psi\rangle = a_0|0\rangle + a_1|1\rangle \tag{1} \end{equation}

Here, a_0 and a_1 are what we call probability amplitudes. They are just coefficients attached to our basic states that tell us "how much" of each state is present in our superposition.

Photons and Vector Notation

For our class, we are specifically looking at photons to represent our qubits. We could use magnets (spin up or down) or electronic charge in a capacitor, but we are going to use the direction of photon polarization.

Let’s assign our physical states to our bits:

  • |0\rangle is equivalent to a horizontally polarized photon, written as |\leftrightarrow\rangle.

  • |1\rangle is equivalent to a vertically polarized photon, written as |\updownarrow\rangle.

Because you have all survived pre-calculus and physics, you are already familiar with vectors. We can translate this abstract quantum speak into handy vector notation. Our horizontal and vertical states can be written as column vectors:

\begin{equation} |\leftrightarrow\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad |\updownarrow\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \tag{2} \end{equation}

This makes intuitive sense, right? For the horizontal vector, the first number (the horizontal component) is 1, and the vertical component is 0. It is entirely horizontal. For the vertical vector, the horizontal component is 0, and the vertical component is 1.

So, our superposition from Equation 1 can be rewritten as a single vector:

\begin{equation} |\psi\rangle = a_0 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + a_1 \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a_0 \\ a_1 \end{pmatrix} \tag{3} \end{equation}

Orthonormal Basis States: The Building Blocks

I threw three big words at you earlier: orthonormal, basis, and states. Let’s break those down, because they are going to be your best friends.

  • Ortho means orthogonal, or perpendicular. Our horizontal and vertical vectors are definitely perpendicular to each other.

  • Normal means having a length (or magnitude) of exactly 1.

  • Basis just means "building blocks."

The vectors |\leftrightarrow\rangle and |\updownarrow\rangle make up a basis because, by linearly combining them, you can draw any polarization direction you want.

Analogies for Intuition

If the math feels a bit dry, let’s look at some everyday analogies for an orthonormal basis:

1. 3D Space: In physics, you describe any position or velocity in 3D space by combining unit vectors along the X, Y, and Z axes (\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z}). Those three vectors form an orthonormal basis for 3D space.

2. Video Game Characters: If you play RPGs, your character is built from a basis of attributes: Strength, Speed, Endurance, Magic, etc. You can create any character archetype by linearly combining different amounts of these base stats.

3. The Culinary Basis: Think about the five basic elements of taste: salty, sweet, bitter, sour, and umami. You cannot get "sweet" out of "salty"—they are independent (orthogonal). But by linearly combining these five basic tastes in different proportions, a chef can create literally any flavor profile in the world!

Shifting Perspectives: Alternative Bases

We call horizontal and vertical the standard orthonormal basis because it is the easiest thing for our brains to picture. But why limit ourselves?

What if, instead of horizontal and vertical, we tilted our heads and used 45-degree angles? Let’s define an "up-diagonal" state (|45^\circ\rangle) and a "down-diagonal" state (|-45^\circ\rangle).

Is there anything wrong with writing our photon state using these as our building blocks? Not at all! They are perpendicular to each other, and as long as we adjust their lengths to be exactly 1, they form a totally legitimate orthonormal basis.

Using a bit of unit-circle trigonometry, we can write these diagonal states in terms of our standard horizontal/vertical vectors:

\begin{equation} |45^\circ\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix}, \quad |-45^\circ\rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ -1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \tag{4} \end{equation}

Let’s double-check that these are normalized (length of 1) using the good old Pythagorean theorem. The length is the square root of the horizontal component squared plus the vertical component squared:

\begin{equation} \text{Length} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{1} = 1 \tag{5} \end{equation}

It checks out! You can represent any photon polarization state as a linear combination of |45^\circ\rangle and |-45^\circ\rangle, using new probability amplitudes (let’s call them a_0' and a_1'):

\begin{equation} |\psi\rangle = a_0'|45^\circ\rangle + a_1'|-45^\circ\rangle \tag{6} \end{equation}

You aren’t even limited to 45 degrees. You could use a 60^\circ and -30^\circ basis. As long as the two vectors are 90 degrees apart (orthogonal) and have a length of 1 (normal), the possibilities are infinite.

The Act of Measurement: Where Things Get Weird

Okay, so we can write our photon state in an infinite number of ways. Why does this matter to us?

You have probably heard that in quantum mechanics, the outcome you get depends on how you measure the system. This concept of basis states is the natural way to explain that phenomenon. When you do a measurement, you are automatically picking which basis you are in.

Let’s look at a physical example using a polarizer. A polarizer is a filter that only lets light through if it is oscillating in a specific direction.

Measuring in the Standard Basis

If I set my polarizer to be exactly horizontal (0^\circ), I am forcing the universe to give me an answer in the standard horizontal/vertical basis. There are only two possible outcomes for a single incident photon: 1. Transmitted: The photon makes it through. We now know with 100% certainty it is horizontal (|\leftrightarrow\rangle). 2. Blocked: The photon does not make it through. We know it must have been vertical (|\updownarrow\rangle).

If we rotate that same polarizer to be vertical (90^\circ), we are still measuring in the standard basis, just testing for the other state.

If a photon is already horizontal, and we hit it with a horizontal polarizer, it passes through flawlessly. If we hit it with a vertical polarizer, it gets blocked entirely. So far, this isn’t too weird. This aligns with our classical intuition.

The 50/50 Split

Here is where the quantum weirdness kicks in. What if we know for a fact that we have a horizontal photon coming in, but we rotate our polarizer to a 45^\circ angle?

The measurement device (the 45^\circ polarizer) dictates the possible outcomes. The photon cannot come out the other side as horizontal. It must choose one of the basis states defined by the measurement: it will either be transmitted as |45^\circ\rangle or blocked (meaning it was |-45^\circ\rangle).

Because a horizontal photon is exactly halfway between 45^\circ and -45^\circ, it faces a 50/50 split.

Here is the key takeaway, and I want you to write this down: The measurement itself automatically sets the possible outcomes. By setting the physical orientation of our polarizer, we are mathematically setting the basis states we can observe.

The Collapse of the Superposition

I mentioned earlier that a 45^\circ photon is a superposition of horizontal and vertical. Let’s look at the math for that again:

\begin{equation} |45^\circ\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|\leftrightarrow\rangle + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|\updownarrow\rangle \tag{7} \end{equation}

Here is the frustrating (but fascinating) part of quantum mechanics: You can never see the superposition directly.

As soon as you try to measure or "see" the photon using a horizontal/vertical polarizer, you disturb it. The superposition collapses. You will only ever get one of the two basis states dictated by your polarizer. It will be either horizontal or vertical, nothing in between.

How do we know which one it will be? We rely on probabilities. The probability of observing a specific state is equal to the square of its probability amplitude:

\begin{equation} \text{Probability} = |\text{Probability Amplitude}|^2 \tag{8} \end{equation}

Let’s test this on our |45^\circ\rangle photon being measured by a horizontal polarizer. The amplitude for the horizontal state |\leftrightarrow\rangle is \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.

\begin{equation} \text{Probability of transmitting} = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} = 50\% \tag{9} \end{equation}

There is a 50% chance the photon makes it through (and becomes horizontal), and a 50% chance it gets blocked (meaning it collapsed into the vertical state).

Testing Our Intuition: The Polarizer Game

To wrap up today, let’s recap the game we played in class to test our intuition on this. We had a "referee" holding a polarizer at a specific angle, and a "measurer" sending in photons at different angles. The goal was to predict the probability of transmission.

If the incoming photon is completely lined up with the polarizer (e.g., 0^\circ photon into a 0^\circ polarizer), transmission is 100%. If it is orthogonal (90^\circ off), transmission is 0%. If it is 45^\circ off, transmission is 50%.

But what if the angle difference is something funky, like 30^\circ? If you remember your unit circle, the horizontal component of a 30^\circ angle is \cos(30^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. That is our probability amplitude. To find the probability of transmission, we just square it:

\begin{equation} \text{Probability} = \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{3}{4} = 75\% \tag{10} \end{equation}

If you can confidently predict the outcomes for 0^\circ, 90^\circ, 45^\circ, and -45^\circ setups, you are in great shape. You have successfully grasped the core weirdness of quantum measurement!

Next time, we are going to take this foundation and use it to talk about something even wilder: quantum entanglement. And yes, there will be candy involved to help us model it. See you then!
